semantic_description: The most common adult contact call; signals contentment and non-aggression during foraging and resting, used to maintain cohesion and communicate well-being within the group.
acoustic_description: A deep, prolonged resonant rumble with a di-syllabic or rolling quality, sometimes described as a soft throat-clearing "ummm-ummm" with the second note falling from the first; produced at moderate amplitude.

semantic_description: Used during travel and group movement to coordinate minimal-disturbance cohesion; also produced in response to mild arousal or uncertainty during routine activity.
acoustic_description: A nasal, pig-like snorting call produced in short bursts, with a rough-voiced or noisy character at low to moderate amplitude.

semantic_description: Produced in response to novel or ambiguous stimuli, functioning as an investigatory alert to probe unknown sounds or mild disturbances before escalating to full alarm.
acoustic_description: A sharp, inquisitive "woof" or hooting bark of brief duration with an abrupt onset, moderate to loud amplitude, and some upward frequency modulation.

semantic_description: The primary alarm vocalization; produced in response to confirmed threats such as predators or sudden severe disturbance, triggering immediate group flight or defensive response.
acoustic_description: An explosive, loud single bark with very abrupt onset and broad noisy spectral energy, acoustically more intense and distinct than the question bark.

semantic_description: Produced by silverback males during dominance displays, charging runs, inter-group encounters, and serious agonistic confrontations; signals maximum arousal and threat.
acoustic_description: A very loud, forceful vocalization with broad spectral energy spanning low to mid frequencies, sustained over one or more seconds, produced with intense respiratory effort.

semantic_description: A mild threat signal directed toward subordinates or rivals at close range; indicates low-level agonistic tension without escalation to full display.
acoustic_description: A low rumbling, gravelly vocalization of brief to moderate duration at low amplitude, with rough-voiced or noisy spectral quality.

semantic_description: Produced during active play, wrestling, and tickling interactions; analogous to human laughter, signaling playful non-aggressive intent.
acoustic_description: A series of short, rapidly pulsed breathy or voiced notes resembling a giggle or laugh, delivered at moderate amplitude with a relaxed, airflow-driven quality.

semantic_description: Emitted by infants and juveniles in distress, separation anxiety, or when soliciting maternal care; also used when a young animal is uncomfortable or seeking reassurance.
acoustic_description: A high-pitched, sustained voiced cry with tonal or weakly harmonic structure, variable in contour, produced at low to moderate amplitude.

semantic_description: Produced predominantly by silverback males, possibly involving laryngeal air sacs; used during display sequences, potentially communicating individual identity or status.
acoustic_description: A series of repeated low-pitched tonal pulses given at a regular rate (approximately 10–11 pulses per second), with a resonant, staccato character; produced at moderate to loud amplitude.

semantic_description: Produced by silverback males and directed toward specific receptive females as a sexual invitation; a courtship-specific variant of the whinny vocalization.
acoustic_description: Acoustically similar to the whinny but with a higher pulse rate (approximately 13 pulses per second); distinguished from the regular whinny by rate and contextual directionality.

semantic_description: Produced by silverback males in mild corrective or threat contexts toward group members, particularly juveniles or females engaged in unwanted behavior; a low-intensity disciplinary signal.
acoustic_description: A brief, sharp cough-like exhalation with noisy broadband character, low amplitude, and very abrupt onset; acoustically intermediate between a cough and a grunt.

semantic_description: Produced by pairs or groups to advertise and defend territories year-round. Dominant male or female typically initiates the first notes; others join in coordinated group display that reinforces group cohesion and signals territory boundaries to neighbouring groups.
acoustic_description: Loud, rich, melodious phrases pitched between approximately 6 and 8 kHz with 4–5 distinct elements and slurring transitions between notes. Frequency-modulated with complex harmonic structure. Phrases can be sustained for many seconds; overall impression is powerful and musical.

semantic_description: Produced when a bird is alone or in relaxed social settings; not directed at rivals or predators. Considered analogous to practice or rehearsal song; also produced in contexts suggesting general well-being or low arousal.
acoustic_description: Soft, undulating, continuous musical phrase pitched at approximately 1–4 kHz with predominantly pure tones and some complex harmonics. Low amplitude; does not carry far. Individual bouts can last up to 70 minutes.

semantic_description: Sung by the group as a coordinated chorus at dawn and dusk, primarily in winter and spring. Thought to reinforce territorial boundaries at the transition between night and day when neighbouring groups may be assessing each other's presence.
acoustic_description: A short, repetitive version of the carolling phrase sung in chorus just before dawn and again at twilight; individually similar in spectral structure to full carolling but phrases are briefer and repeated in rapid succession.

semantic_description: Produced in response to intrusions by rival groups or unfamiliar conspecifics; also used to reinforce group cohesion. Contains information about group identity and size that can be assessed by neighbouring groups.
acoustic_description: Overlapping carolling phrases produced simultaneously by multiple group members, creating a rich layered soundscape. Individual contributions remain tonally similar to solo carol but the combined output is louder and more spectrally dense.

semantic_description: Functionally referential signal specific to overhead aerial predators, especially eagles. Elicits scanning behaviour and crouching or shelter-seeking in group members. Distinguished from other alarm types by receivers, who respond differently to it than to ground-predator alarms.
acoustic_description: Complex, tonal call of more than two syllables; overall high-pitched with rapid frequency modulation between elements. Distinctly different in structure from ground-predator alarm; elicited most consistently by large raptors such as eagles.

semantic_description: Produced in response to terrestrial predators (snakes, cats, dogs, raptors on the ground). Recruits group members to mob the predator; elicits approach and mobbing behaviour rather than the flight/hiding response typical of aerial alarms.
acoustic_description: Harsh, staccato squawk; broadband and noisy with abrupt onset and offset. Shorter duration than aerial alarm elements. Often repeated rapidly in series when the threat remains present.

semantic_description: Used as a general alert when a potential but unspecified threat is detected. Triggers increased vigilance in group members without eliciting the specific avoidance or mobbing response of referential alarm calls.
acoustic_description: Brief, single high-pitched note of short duration. Acoustically simpler than the referential aerial or ground alarm calls; may precede more specific alarm sequences or occur in ambiguous threat contexts.

semantic_description: Directed at intruding conspecifics or humans approaching a nest. Common during swooping behaviour in the breeding season. Also used in intragroup dominance interactions to displace subordinates from food or perches.
acoustic_description: Harsh, loud broadband squawk or series of squawks with noisy, atonal quality. May include bill snapping. Abrupt in onset and often repeated during or immediately before physical attack.

semantic_description: Produced to maintain contact with group members within the territory when visual contact is intermittent. Allows individuals to track the location of conspecifics during foraging without triggering territorial or alarm responses.
acoustic_description: Short, relatively pure-toned note of moderate pitch; softer than alarm or aggressive calls. May be graded in intensity depending on distance from group members.

semantic_description: Produced by fledglings and juveniles to solicit food from parents or other group members. Elicits regurgitation or prey-delivery behaviour in adults. Continues beyond nutritional independence in some individuals, gradually decreasing in frequency as juveniles become more self-sufficient.
acoustic_description: Repeated, short, high-pitched call with slightly whining or nasal tonal quality. Graded in rate and intensity; higher repetition rates associated with greater hunger or proximity of a parent.

semantic_description: Australian Magpies are accomplished vocal mimics capable of incorporating sounds from dozens of species and environmental sounds into their song. Function debated: hypotheses include mate attraction, individual identity signals, and territory advertisement. Mimicry content varies among individuals and groups.
acoustic_description: Acoustically variable, closely matching the source species or sound; may include songs and calls of other birds, mammal sounds, and anthropogenic sounds. Incorporated into and around song phrases; spectral and temporal parameters reflect the imitated source rather than a fixed magpie-typical structure.

semantic_description: Produced at territorial boundaries during low-level disputes, or when a bird is aware of but not yet alarmed by a neighbouring group. Functions as a lower-cost signal of territorial presence before escalating to full carol or aggressive call.
acoustic_description: A quieter, less elaborate version of the full territorial carol; spectral structure similar but amplitude and phrase length reduced. Directed toward specific locations such as territorial boundaries or specific rival individuals.

semantic_description: Non-song calls that exhibit two levels of combinatoriality: individual acoustic segments are combined into discrete call types, which are further combined into call sequences. Used across a range of social contexts including territory defence, intragroup competition, antipredator behaviour, and recruitment. Production is linked to the composition of the immediate social environment.
acoustic_description: Four acoustically distinct segments (labelled A, B, C, D in published work) recombined into a larger set of calls, which are in turn combined into call sequences. Individual segments range from tonal to noisy; combined output is multi-component and variable in spectral structure depending on segment ordering.

semantic_description: Produced by juveniles as they acquire the full territorial repertoire through vocal learning. Evidence suggests juveniles face social constraints on where and when they can sing in the presence of dominant adults, particularly regarding calls directed at neighbours versus strangers.
acoustic_description: Acoustically similar to adult carolling but less precise in frequency contour and phrase structure; shows developmental errors and rehearsal-like variability. Gradually converges on adult form over the first one to two years of life.

semantic_description: Produced when a bird is captured or physically attacked. Recruits nearby group members who may mob the attacker. Distinct from alarm calls in that it signals active physical distress rather than the presence of a potential threat.
acoustic_description: Loud, harsh, high-pitched scream with broadband noisy quality. Produced with high intensity; clearly distinguishable from alarm or aggressive calls by greater amplitude and more continuous structure.

semantic_description: Used as a routine greeting and contact call that conveys individual and colony membership in the dark tunnel system.
acoustic_description: A brief, soft, high-pitched tonal call, often emitted in stereotyped call-and-response exchanges and showing colony-specific acoustic patterning.

semantic_description: Used in ordinary close-range colony interactions and spatial coordination underground.
acoustic_description: A short low call with simple structure and lower amplitude than alarm-like calls.

semantic_description: Produced in acute conflict, rough handling, or discomfort.
acoustic_description: A sharper, louder call than routine soft chirps or grunts, with abrupt onset and harsher spectral quality.

semantic_description: Used in close-range dominance, aggressive encounters, or direct social challenge inside the tunnel system.
acoustic_description: A brief harsh broadband exhalatory call with noisier structure than chirps or grunts and an abrupt onset.

semantic_description: Used to alert colony members to immediate disturbance or danger in the tunnel system.
acoustic_description: A conspicuous abrupt loud call type distinct from routine contact vocalizations and suited to travel through tunnels.

semantic_description: Included conservatively as a juvenile solicitation class expected in the cooperative breeding colony system.
acoustic_description: Repeated higher-pitched calls from pups that are more urgent and attention-getting than adult routine contact chirps.

semantic_description: Included as a broad call class used to draw colony members toward food discoveries or feeding opportunities in the burrow system.
acoustic_description: A low-frequency recruiting call louder and more insistent than ordinary contact chirps, suited for broadcasting through tunnels.

semantic_description: Included as a colony-coordination call used in the communal toilet context reported for this species' broad vocal repertoire.
acoustic_description: A repeated low call class presumed to be simpler and less intense than alarm or distress calls.

semantic_description: Included conservatively as a reproductive call category reported in broad species accounts of the naked mole-rat repertoire.
acoustic_description: A lower-frequency, socially directed reproductive call class expected to be more prolonged and patterned than brief contact chirps.

semantic_description: Produced in response to more urgent or distant disturbances; functions as a long-range alerting call that complements the short-range soft chirp and alarm shriek.
acoustic_description: A louder variant of the soft chirp with higher amplitude, capable of traveling farther through tunnels (estimated up to 15 m at suprathreshold intensities). Shares the brief tonal structure of the soft chirp but is clearly audible at greater distances.

semantic_description: Produced in close social interactions; noted as one of the named call types from early observations of continuously vocalizing colony members in tunnel systems.
acoustic_description: A rapid series of brief frequency-modulated notes producing a twittering or trilling percept; higher-pitched and more rapid than the discrete soft chirp, often blending into a continuous acoustic stream.

semantic_description: Produced in intense distress, acute pain, or severe social conflict; more extreme in urgency than the squeak and likely recruits stronger colony responses.
acoustic_description: A prolonged, high-pitched, often frequency-modulated call louder and more sustained than the brief squeak; harsh spectral quality with notable amplitude.

semantic_description: A close-range threat signal used in agonistic interactions, dominance contests, and defense; the prominent incisors of naked mole-rats make this a plausible threat display mechanism reported for bathyergid rodents.
acoustic_description: A pulsed rattling sound produced by rapid incisor contact; broadband and percussive in quality, distinct from purely laryngeal calls.

semantic_description: A rare call attributed to the queen in the communal toilet chamber; function is not yet fully understood but may serve a group-coordination or identity-signaling role in the colony.
acoustic_description: A distinctive call series produced by the queen in the communal toilet chamber context; specific spectro-temporal details are not well-documented in the literature, described anecdotally as a brief song-like sequence.

semantic_description: Produced when pups are separated from the group or from caregivers; distinct from the generalized pup begging call in being driven by isolation rather than nutritional solicitation.
acoustic_description: A high-pitched brief call produced by isolated or separated pups; higher frequency and more intense than routine contact calls, possibly with ultrasonic components reaching above 10 kHz.

semantic_description: Produced during encounters with individuals from foreign colonies; naked mole-rats discriminate colony membership via soft chirp dialect, and unfamiliar individuals trigger agonistic vocal and physical responses.
acoustic_description: A harsh loud brief call produced when encountering unfamiliar individuals; characterized by broadband spectral content and abrupt onset distinct from routine colony contact calls.

semantic_description: Produced by subordinates in yielding or deferential encounters; part of the graded acoustic repertoire associated with social rank signaling in the eusocial colony.
acoustic_description: A sustained tonal call with a falling or variable frequency contour; higher-pitched and more drawn-out than a grunt, with relatively low amplitude.

semantic_description: Associated with the ritualized shoving interactions that facilitate movement coordination in narrow tunnel passageways; may convey rank or passage-request information among colony members.
acoustic_description: A brief low-amplitude grunt-like sound produced during the stereotyped shoving behavior when colony members pass each other in narrow tunnels; likely a graded acoustic signal blending with physical contact.

semantic_description: Used by males to attract females in breeding choruses.
acoustic_description: A repeated breeding-season call with stable tonal structure and stereotyped pulse pattern.

semantic_description: Used in close-range male-male interactions around calling sites.
acoustic_description: A shorter more forceful call than the advertisement call, directed to nearby rivals.

semantic_description: Used in male-male competition and territorial escalation around calling sites.
acoustic_description: A harsher and more forceful local call than the advertisement call, used in escalated male interactions.

semantic_description: Signals inappropriate amplexus and prompts release.
acoustic_description: A brief call produced during unwanted physical contact or clasping.

semantic_description: Used by males to attract females in breeding choruses.
acoustic_description: A repeated nasal or quank-like breeding call with fairly stable temporal structure.

semantic_description: Used in close-range male-male interactions around calling positions.
acoustic_description: A shorter more forceful call than the advertisement call, directed to nearby rivals.

semantic_description: Used in disturbance and warning contexts and distinguished behaviorally from advertisement and release calling.
acoustic_description: A shorter and more urgent call than the advertisement signal, with a harsher defensive quality.

semantic_description: Produced when frogs appear to sense imminent rain, outside the direct mate-attraction context of the advertisement call.
acoustic_description: A distinct non-advertisement call type reported as different from mating, warning, and release calls, but with limited accessible detail on its exact spectro-temporal structure.

semantic_description: Signals inappropriate amplexus and prompts release.
acoustic_description: A brief protest call produced during unwanted physical contact or clasping.

semantic_description: Used by pair-bonded adults for long-range territorial advertisement, pair cohesion, and neighbour assessment.
acoustic_description: A prolonged coordinated song with repeated phrase patterns and contributions from both pair members, often delivered as a structured bout over several minutes.

semantic_description: A prominent female-led display element in duet performance and territorial advertisement.
acoustic_description: A distinctive high-amplitude phrase with strong pitch modulation and far-carrying tonal structure, typically the most stereotyped female song element.

semantic_description: Contributes to coordinated duet structure and pair-level or male-specific song identity.
acoustic_description: A sequence of shorter terminal notes or phrase endings that contrasts with the longer female great-call section.

semantic_description: Used for long-range advertisement when a pair mate is absent or when individuals sing alone during territorial signalling.
acoustic_description: A prolonged loud song structurally related to duet material but produced by a single caller, usually with repeated phrase types and strong tonality.

semantic_description: Produced in response to dangerous animals and serves to alert nearby group members while coordinating a collective reaction.
acoustic_description: A more abrupt and harsher song-like bout than the routine duet, with repeated forceful notes and reduced smoothness.

semantic_description: Used in high-arousal local contexts outside the core song bout, including sudden disturbance.
acoustic_description: A short bark-like call with abrupt onset and harsher structure than the main tonal song elements.

semantic_description: Produced by both sexes during feeding, separation from group members, predator encounters, neighbour interactions, and sometimes within duet contexts; best treated as the main quiet social call of the species rather than split into several separate named calls.
acoustic_description: A soft low-amplitude close-range call with relatively little spectral complexity, but with subtle acoustic variation across contexts.

semantic_description: Used in territorial advertisement, pair or family cohesion, and long-range social display.
acoustic_description: A prolonged often group-coordinated song composed of repeated phrase patterns, strong harmonic structure, and alternation among several phrase types.

semantic_description: A recurring song unit that likely contributes to caller or group distinctiveness within long-range advertisement.
acoustic_description: A stereotyped tonal phrase with clear harmonic energy and a descending frequency contour, commonly embedded in the broader song.

semantic_description: Given especially to aerial predators and also as an introductory element of songs, making it both an alarm and long-range display component.
acoustic_description: A forceful harsh vocal element with stronger noisy energy than the more tonal song sections.

semantic_description: Used mainly against terrestrial predators or other dangerous intruders, including humans in non-habituated groups.
acoustic_description: A series of short loud tonal notes, often rhythmic and sometimes preceded by a voiced inhalation.

semantic_description: Used during rest, foraging, and travel to maintain close contact within the group.
acoustic_description: A low-intensity low-pitched call, often produced repeatedly back-to-back with little carrying power.

semantic_description: Produced in vigilance and stress-related contexts, often before songs or as the opening element of the kiss-wheeze cry sometimes called the cri d'amour.
acoustic_description: A brief percussive click-like or smacking local call with abrupt onset and little tonal structure.

semantic_description: Used in vigilance, intragroup competition, and responses to potentially dangerous or noxious stimuli.
acoustic_description: A rapid exhaled call, often paired with a preceding kiss and acoustically more breathy and noisy than tonal short-range calls.

semantic_description: Produced in agonistic interactions and often emitted as a sequence during physical conflict between group members.
acoustic_description: A longer tonal call with clearer pitch structure and greater duration than the short tonal call.

semantic_description: Used in physical aggression and often interspersed between long tonal calls during intragroup conflicts.
acoustic_description: A short harsh tonal call, briefer and sharper than the long tonal call.

semantic_description: Used in tense, vigilance, and agonistic situations, including intragroup conflict and warning contexts.
acoustic_description: A short low-pitched pulsed call, often given in series and with less carrying power than roars, honks, or songs.

semantic_description: Included as a plausible mixed short-range arousal call reported in later repertoire-level comparisons; likely used in tense close-contact situations where grunt- and wheeze-like signals blend.
acoustic_description: A short low-amplitude call intermediate between a grunt and a wheeze, combining pulsed low-frequency energy with a breathier exhaled quality.

semantic_description: Treated here as a distinct song-related call class because later indri repertoire summaries list it separately from the full song, although its boundary from embedded song phrases remains fuzzy.
acoustic_description: A brief tonal unit extracted from the song system, shorter and more modular than a full song bout and retaining the harmonic phrase-like quality of song notes.

semantic_description: Used by males in territory advertisement and mate attraction.
acoustic_description: A repeated trilled song phrase with relatively stereotyped structure.

semantic_description: Used in everyday communication and mild disturbance contexts.
acoustic_description: A brief sharp call with simple structure and clear onset.

semantic_description: Used in higher-alert or more urgent disturbance situations.
acoustic_description: A thinner higher-pitched call than the chip with urgent quality.

semantic_description: Helps coordinate movement and maintain awareness during displacement.
acoustic_description: A brief call given in movement contexts, generally simple and suited to short-range contact.

semantic_description: Used in ordinary flock awareness and close-range social interaction.
acoustic_description: A brief everyday call with simpler structure than songs and urgent alarm notes.

semantic_description: Used in aggressive spacing interactions and appears to encourage nearby birds to move apart.
acoustic_description: A sharp musical single-note call, clearer and more individually discrete than the routine chip note.

semantic_description: Heard during altercations or when birds flush suddenly.
acoustic_description: A fast series of several short notes delivered in a tight burst during agitated moments.

semantic_description: Used by nestlings or fledglings to solicit food and parental care.
acoustic_description: A repeated thin call delivered persistently by dependent young, simpler than adult songs and local calls.

semantic_description: Produced at close range by both sexes in low-intensity social or pair contexts rather than in long-range territorial advertisement.
acoustic_description: A lower-amplitude series of whistles, trills, and warbles with looser phrase structure than the loud stereotyped trill song.

semantic_description: Used in close social contact and low-arousal affiliative situations, and may signal nonaggressive intent.
acoustic_description: A soft low-amplitude rhythmic vocalization with relatively even tonal pulses and little harsh noise.

semantic_description: Used to maintain contact and coordinate group spacing, especially when individuals are separated over moderate distance.
acoustic_description: A clearer and more prolonged tonal call than the purr, often with marked pitch modulation and strong harmonic structure.

semantic_description: Common in close social interactions involving solicitation, dependent young, or approach to social partners.
acoustic_description: A sustained lower-pitched tonal call with smoother and more plaintive structure than the meow.

semantic_description: Functions in long-range spacing, group assembly, and social display.
acoustic_description: A loud prolonged call or call series with sustained tonal energy, often more forceful and far-carrying than routine contact calls.

semantic_description: Common in agonistic interactions and mild fear contexts, often signalling deference or social unease.
acoustic_description: A short sharp high-pitched call with abrupt onset and a more urgent quality than soft contact calls.

semantic_description: Produced in defensive or escalated agonistic situations and may reflect readiness to resist or retaliate.
acoustic_description: A harsh repeated call series with noisy structure and a defensive rattling quality.

semantic_description: Associated with fearful but socially engaged interactions and used in agonistic exchanges where individuals remain near each other.
acoustic_description: A rapid series of short high notes with a lighter more tonal structure than harsher aggressive calls.

semantic_description: Produced during stronger distress, separation, or handling, especially in situations likely to recruit social support or care.
acoustic_description: A louder more prolonged distress call than the yip, with rising or wavering high-frequency energy.

semantic_description: A high-intensity threat or alarm signal produced during serious disturbance, conflict, or sudden danger.
acoustic_description: A loud explosive broad-spectrum bark with abrupt onset and little tonal continuity.

semantic_description: Used in group positioning, relocation, and travel-related coordination, especially as an affiliative contact signal during movement.
acoustic_description: A short bright note or brief series of notes, typically higher and lighter than meows or moans.

semantic_description: Used in agonistic or fearful social interactions, often as a lower-intensity submissive or uneasy signal distinct from louder alarm barking.
acoustic_description: A rough repeated close-range call series that is harsher and more sputtering than the twitter.

semantic_description: A male-specific call used in both agonistic and sexual contexts, making it a socially conspicuous signal during rivalry and reproductive interactions.
acoustic_description: A sharp high-pitched call with a piercing tonal quality and stronger amplitude than most routine contact calls.

semantic_description: Produced before slow group relocation or to maintain cohesion with nearby group members in low-arousal settings.
acoustic_description: A soft low-amplitude nasal-sounding call, usually shorter and less modulated than the moan or meow.

semantic_description: Included as a probable short-range movement or relocation signal mentioned in broader species accounts, though its boundary from other low-amplitude cohesion calls remains uncertain.
acoustic_description: A brief low-pitched note with a compact shape and less carrying power than meows, howls, or wails.

semantic_description: A repulsion or spacing signal produced between two individuals; functions to increase inter-individual distance in mildly agonistic or competitive encounters, distinct from the louder alarm barking used in predator contexts.
acoustic_description: A low-pitched rough pulsed note delivered singly or as a staccato series; less broadband and explosively forceful than the plosive bark, with a guttural rasping quality at relatively moderate amplitude.

semantic_description: A generalized group-alert vocalization produced upon detecting a potential predator or disturbance; appears to function as a low-urgency broadcast signal that puts group members on alert without specifying predator type or direction.
acoustic_description: A brief soft relatively low-pitched note with a gulping or swallowing quality, distinct from the louder plosive bark in amplitude and spectral breadth.

semantic_description: A referential aerial-predator alarm call produced selectively in response to raptors (hawks, eagles); directs group members to look upward and seek lower shelter in vegetation.
acoustic_description: A harsh rasping broadband note, rougher and more sputtering than the plosive bark, often produced in rapid sequences with a scratchy textured quality.

semantic_description: An aerial-predator alarm call, also used in high-urgency disturbance contexts; may function both to warn group members and to signal to a detected raptor that it has been seen, potentially deterring attack.
acoustic_description: A loud high-pitched call with a piercing quality, higher and more intense in frequency than most contact or agonistic calls; may grade into noisy broadband components at peak intensity.

semantic_description: Produced during predator encounters; rates are elevated in populations facing higher predator pressure and functions as part of the alarm-mobbing complex alongside rasp and shriek.
acoustic_description: A sharp staccato bark-like note, shorter and higher-pitched than the plosive bark but retaining a broad-spectrum noisy quality; often produced in rapid series.

semantic_description: A low-arousal location-marker call that advertises the caller's spatial position to nearby group members; used by all age classes except very young infants and functions to regulate close-range spacing during foraging and rest.
acoustic_description: A very brief broadband mechanical-sounding impulsive note produced as a single click or in loose irregular sequences; very short duration and low amplitude compared to alarm calls.

semantic_description: A moderate-arousal location-marker call; produced in situations of greater urgency or social tension than single clicks but without reaching the high-arousal contexts of open-mouth click series or alarm calls.
acoustic_description: A rapid pulsed series of clicks produced with the mouth closed, generating a machine-gun-like repetitive pattern at moderate amplitude; faster and more continuous than single click sequences.

semantic_description: A high-arousal location-marker and alert call produced during significant disturbances; signals the caller's position under conditions of elevated fear or social tension, bridging location-marking and alarm functions.
acoustic_description: A rapid series of clicks produced with the mouth open, louder and with broader spectral content than the CMCS; the high-arousal click series has a rougher harsher texture due to the open-mouth posture.

semantic_description: Produced during intergroup encounters and while traveling to facilitate group cohesion, territory advertisement, and intergroup spacing. Also used for within-group coordination when members are separated. Individuals can be identified from long-call structure.
acoustic_description: Loud, multi-phrase call typically lasting 3–8 seconds and spanning approximately 4–12 kHz. Begins with an introductory syllable (chirp, trill, or whine) followed by one to three structurally distinct phrases in fixed sequential order; each phrase consists of characteristic syllables of ascending frequency. Highly tonal with clear harmonic structure.

semantic_description: Used to communicate location and maintain contact over moderate to long distances while traveling or foraging. Also used during solo activity. Can serve as an introductory note in long calls.
acoustic_description: Rapid series of frequency-modulated tonal notes producing a rolling, buzzing quality. Relatively high-pitched (roughly 5–10 kHz), short individual elements repeated in quick succession. Duration of bouts variable but individual notes are brief.

semantic_description: Versatile call used in affiliative interactions within the group, as an alarm response to predators, during food sharing, and as the introductory note of long calls. The context modulates its precise structure and intensity.
acoustic_description: Long, rising or falling tonal note; clearly whistled and relatively pure in tone. Frequency modulated with a sweep contour, typically in the 5–12 kHz range. Duration of individual notes is relatively long compared to clucks or peeps. Graded in intensity.

semantic_description: Produced during foraging excursions and in the presence of food. Functions to signal food availability and recruit group members. Also emitted during mild agonistic encounters.
acoustic_description: Short, abrupt, broad-spectrum note with limited tonal quality. Relatively low frequency compared to trills and whines; individual notes are brief and often repeated in sequences. Has a clicking or chuck-like character.

semantic_description: Emitted when an individual sees or possesses food. Recruits other group members to the food source. Provides referential-like information about food presence.
acoustic_description: High-pitched chattering vocalization with a peak frequency around 5 kHz. Consists of rapidly repeated short, tonal or semi-tonal notes. Structurally distinct from the cluck in its higher frequency and more tonal character.

semantic_description: Produced when an individual actively offers food to another group member, especially to juveniles and infants. Recipient typically approaches the caller and accepts food with little resistance. Proposed to function in teaching food recognition to young.
acoustic_description: Variable tonal vocalization emitted after or in combination with a food call. Acoustic structure is more variable than the food call, with greater frequency modulation. Graded in form, suggesting context sensitivity.

semantic_description: Produced by juveniles and infants, particularly while begging for food from group members as they transition to solid food. Also emitted by youngsters during play. Adults may use it in low-intensity distress or mild agonistic contexts.
acoustic_description: Harsh, noisy, broadband vocalization with a rasping or buzzing quality. Relatively aperiodic, lacking clear tonal structure. Short in duration, may be emitted singly or in brief bouts.

semantic_description: Associated with affiliative interactions and alliance signaling within the group. Functions to maintain social bonds and close-range contact. May signal appeasement or friendly intent.
acoustic_description: Very short, high-pitched tonal note. Simple in structure, relatively quiet, and brief. Frequency content is high (often above 7 kHz). Can be emitted singly or in sparse series.

semantic_description: Associated with alarm contexts and heightened vigilance. May function as a low-level alert or attention-directing call in response to potential threats or disturbances.
acoustic_description: Very short, sharp, broadband note with a click-like or tick character. Brief onset and offset, high frequency emphasis. Structurally distinct from peeps in its more abrupt and noisy quality.

semantic_description: Produced specifically in response to aerial predators such as raptors and hawks. Elicits rapid descent and hiding behavior from group members. Distinct from terrestrial alarm calls in acoustic structure.
acoustic_description: High-pitched, relatively short tonal or semi-tonal vocalization with abrupt onset. Differs acoustically from terrestrial predator alarm calls. Often a sharp whistle-like note or brief series of notes in the upper frequency range.

semantic_description: Given in response to terrestrial and arboreal predators (e.g., snakes, felids, mustelids). Elicits different escape responses than aerial alarms, typically causing the group to ascend and freeze or mob.
acoustic_description: Harsh, noisy, broadband alarm vocalization with rapid onset. Tends to be lower in frequency and noisier than aerial alarm calls, reflecting the different signal requirements for terrestrial versus aerial predator threats.

semantic_description: Used in contact and coordination contexts. Functions to maintain cohesion during travel or foraging. Also serves as the introductory note of long calls in some individuals, contributing to long-call structural variation.
acoustic_description: Short, sharp, high-pitched tonal note. Brief in duration with a clean onset. Higher in frequency than clucks, purer in tone than rasps. Often used as an introductory syllable in long calls.

semantic_description: Produced in extreme distress or fear situations, including intense predator threat, capture, or severe agonistic encounters. Alerts group members to immediate danger or signals the caller's distress state.
acoustic_description: Loud, harsh, broadband shriek with energy across a wide frequency range. Strongly noisy and aperiodic. High in intensity and typically brief but piercing.

semantic_description: Emitted during aggressive encounters between group members or during intergroup confrontations. Signals threat and offensive intent. Intensity and rate may be graded with level of arousal.
acoustic_description: Harsh, barking or rasping vocalization produced in agonistic contexts. Broad spectrum with noisy quality. Short individual notes that may be repeated in rapid succession during escalated interactions.

semantic_description: Produced by subordinate individuals in response to aggression or approach by dominant group members. Signals appeasement and non-threatening intent, helping to de-escalate agonistic interactions.
acoustic_description: Soft, quiet, high-pitched tonal note or brief series of notes. Lacks the harsh quality of agonistic calls. Low amplitude, relatively pure frequency content.

semantic_description: Produced by infants that become separated from carriers or the group. Elicits retrieval and caregiving behavior from parents and allomaternal caretakers, which are common in this cooperatively breeding species.
acoustic_description: High-pitched, long, repeated tonal call produced by isolated or separated infants. Loud and carrying relative to infant size. Distinctly higher in frequency and more sustained than adult contact calls.

semantic_description: Emitted by infants and juveniles during social play behavior. Function is unclear beyond marking playful motivation; may signal play intent and help sustain play interactions with siblings or parents.
acoustic_description: Irregular, noisy vocalizations of variable structure emitted during play bouts. Not as harsh or loud as distress calls; often mixed with rasps. Short, repeated elements without stereotyped tonal structure.

semantic_description: Produced during allogrooming bouts and other close affiliative interactions. Reinforces social bonds within the family group. May signal positive affective state and maintain proximity between individuals.
acoustic_description: Soft, quiet, tonal short notes emitted during close social contact such as allogrooming. Very low amplitude, nearly whispered quality. Graded in intensity with level of social arousal.

semantic_description: Prominent underwater display signal, especially associated with breeding-season advertisement.
acoustic_description: A long downward-sweeping trill with strong tonal structure and repeated fine modulation, typically in a lower frequency band than high trills.

semantic_description: Used in underwater display and advertisement, likely overlapping functionally with lower trills.
acoustic_description: A long trill with similar repeated modulated structure to the low trill but concentrated in a much higher frequency band, sometimes extending into ultrasonic range.

semantic_description: Used in local social communication.
acoustic_description: A shorter higher-pitched call than trills, often occurring in repeated series with decreasing intervals.

semantic_description: Used in underwater social communication and likely helps maintain spacing or caller recognition.
acoustic_description: A series of discrete upswept whistle elements forming a structured sequence, often followed by a contrasting terminal component.

semantic_description: Used as a simpler local signal within the broader underwater social repertoire.
acoustic_description: A brief single upswept whistle with clearer isolated contour than the multi-element whistle series.

semantic_description: Associated with conflict or aroused close-range encounters.
acoustic_description: A rough lower-frequency call with noisier structure and more threat-like quality than whistles or trills.

semantic_description: Used in underwater advertisement and conspicuous social signalling.
acoustic_description: A two-element tonal call with a long low-frequency component ending in a slowly rising upswept component.

semantic_description: Used in nearby social signalling and likely in rapid attention-getting contexts.
acoustic_description: A short two-part call beginning with an abrupt downsweep followed by a brief lower-frequency tone.

semantic_description: Used in local underwater social communication.
acoustic_description: A series of discrete low-frequency grunts delivered at fairly regular intervals.

semantic_description: Male underwater territorial display during breeding season; part of the three-tier roar series used for agonistic advertisement.
acoustic_description: A broad-bandwidth low-frequency roaring sound, the lowest in pitch of the three roar variants, with rough noisy character and sustained duration.

semantic_description: Male underwater territorial display during breeding season, functionally similar to the other roar types.
acoustic_description: A broad-bandwidth roaring sound in the mid-frequency range, intermediate between the low and high roar types in spectral placement.

semantic_description: Male underwater territorial display, forming part of the three-tier roar series described by Thomas & Kuechle 1982.
acoustic_description: A broad-bandwidth roaring sound concentrated in a higher frequency range than the low and middle roars; still noisy in character with sustained duration.

semantic_description: Underwater display signal; a recognised variant of the trill class in the Thomas & Kuechle taxonomy.
acoustic_description: A narrow-bandwidth trill preceded by a constant-frequency introductory segment; the constant-frequency start distinguishes it from plain trills which begin immediately with frequency modulation.

semantic_description: Underwater social communication signal; used in close-range and mid-range interaction.
acoustic_description: A brief sinusoidal whistle with a clearly descending frequency contour, lasting less than 2 seconds; cleaner and more tonal than roars.

semantic_description: Underwater social communication signal; both sexes produce ascending whistles, though males have larger repertoires.
acoustic_description: A brief sinusoidal whistle with a clearly ascending frequency contour; mirror image in direction to the descending whistle type.

semantic_description: Underwater display signal; the combined structure may encode additional information compared with the constituent elements alone.
acoustic_description: A compound two-element call consisting of a brief ascending whistle followed immediately by a guttural glug or grunt; the two elements alternate in a regular pattern and the coupling is tight enough to be treated as a single call type.

semantic_description: Used in underwater social communication; named for its resemblance to a cat's mew when played back at reduced speed.
acoustic_description: A two-phase call with an abrupt sharp frequency descent at the start followed by a long constant-frequency tonal ending; the transition from steep sweep to stable tone distinguishes it from the chug (which has a brief rather than long constant-frequency ending).

semantic_description: Used in underwater close-range signalling; also appears as the terminal element of the whistle-ascending-grunt compound call.
acoustic_description: A brief descending-frequency call lower in pitch than the chug, with a guttural quality; very short duration and a sharp descending contour with irregular noisy structure.

semantic_description: Underwater display signal; functions as a simple tonal advertisement or spacing signal.
acoustic_description: A sustained, predominantly constant-frequency sinusoidal call with minimal frequency modulation; the simplest tonal call type in the repertoire, often narrow in bandwidth.

semantic_description: Produced underwater in agonistic and display contexts; documented in multiple Weddell seal acoustic studies.
acoustic_description: A short harsh low-frequency call with rapid amplitude modulation giving a buzzing quality; broader bandwidth than trills and with little tonal purity.

semantic_description: Produced in close-range agonistic encounters, typically by males defending underwater territories; classified as an accessory sound rather than a vocalization sensu stricto in some taxonomies.
acoustic_description: A brief impulsive broadband transient produced by rapid closure of the jaws; not a true laryngeal vocalization but a mechanically produced acoustic signal, creating a sharp click-like percussive sound.

semantic_description: Produced underwater in recurrent stereotyped call-type patterns; behavioral function unknown but hypothesized to relate to short-range communication or echolocation.
acoustic_description: A brief frequency-modulated chirp with center frequency at or above 20 kHz; descending chirps have been documented with onset frequencies reaching ~50 kHz, placing the entire element in the ultrasonic range.

semantic_description: Produced in recurrent stereotyped patterns; function not yet established, but may serve short-range signalling functions inaudible to most predators.
acoustic_description: A whistle-like tonal element with fundamental frequency at or above 20 kHz; one whistle element has been recorded reaching 44.2 kHz. Harmonic overtones can extend above 200 kHz.

semantic_description: Detected in two years of continuous recordings at McMurdo Sound; function unknown but analogous context to audible trills suggests display or territorial signalling.
acoustic_description: A frequency-modulated trill with fundamental frequency exceeding 20 kHz; structurally similar to audible trills but shifted entirely into the ultrasonic range.

semantic_description: Documented as a distinct whistle subtype in broadband recordings; may serve similar functions to other whistle variants.
acoustic_description: A whistle with a U-shaped frequency contour: descending and then ascending to produce a concave frequency trace on a spectrogram; the bottom of the U may be relatively brief or sustained.

semantic_description: Produced singly or in sequences as part of multi-element call types; documented in both audible and ultrasonic frequency ranges.
acoustic_description: A short frequency-modulated element with a steeply descending contour; typically brief (tens of milliseconds) and can occur at audible or ultrasonic frequencies, with some elements beginning near 50 kHz.

semantic_description: Produced at the surface by pups to maintain proximity with the mother and to signal nutritional need; used for mother-pup recognition.
acoustic_description: A brief in-air vocalization with mean maximum frequency around 386 Hz and mean minimum around 217 Hz; relatively simple tonal call with some frequency modulation; individually variable enough for maternal recognition after approximately 2 weeks of age.

semantic_description: Produced at the surface to maintain the mother-pup bond; shown to vary geographically between McMurdo Sound and Vestfold Hills populations.
acoustic_description: An in-air tonal call produced by nursing females toward their pups; acoustic structure includes fundamental frequency and harmonic components in the low-to-mid audio range; geographic variation in fundamental frequency parameters has been documented between populations.

semantic_description: Part of the in-air multi-element call sequence; adults and both sexes produce at least 8 in-air call types, of which this is the highest-frequency representative.
acoustic_description: A high-pitched in-air tonal call exceeding 5 kHz produced by adults and pups; can be produced with mouth and nostrils closed, suggesting laryngeal or nasal resonance origin; among the highest-pitched elements of the in-air call repertoire.

semantic_description: Part of the in-air multi-element call sequence; up to 6 call types can be strung together in highly variable sequences.
acoustic_description: A brief in-air low-frequency grunt below approximately 0.2 kHz; the lowest-pitched in-air call type, produced with mouth and nostrils closed; contrasts sharply in frequency with in-air whistles.

semantic_description: Documented as one of the 8+ in-air call types; structurally similar to underwater trills and included in the variable multi-element in-air call sequences.
acoustic_description: An in-air frequency-modulated trill analogous to the underwater trill types but produced in air; similar repeated modulation structure but likely at different frequencies given the different medium.

semantic_description: Produced underwater by males during breeding season; part of the extended display repertoire; may overlap with some trill subtypes in the Thomas & Kuechle taxonomy.
acoustic_description: A slowly frequency-modulated tonal call with a warbling or undulating frequency contour; slower and broader in modulation pattern than trills; intermediate between a trill and a simple whistle in temporal structure.

semantic_description: Produced underwater in territorial and agonistic contexts; classified in some accounts as an accessory sound accompanying display sequences.
acoustic_description: A brief broadband impulsive transient with abrupt onset and rapid decay, acoustically similar to a knocking sound; distinct from jaw claps in that it may originate from laryngeal or sinus mechanisms rather than jaw mechanics.

semantic_description: Produced underwater; function not well established, possibly short-range attention or spacing signal; included in the 34-type Thomas & Kuechle classification as an accessory-type sound.
acoustic_description: A single brief wideband impulse shorter than a knock; may occur as isolated events or in loose series; distinguished from jaw claps by mechanical origin and from trills by the absence of frequency modulation.

semantic_description: Produced by males in underwater territorial display and possibly courtship; extreme ascending contour may signal arousal or dominance.
acoustic_description: A loud ascending tonal call with a steeply rising frequency contour spanning a broad frequency range; more extreme in sweep rate and amplitude than the ascending whistle; screaming quality at playback.

semantic_description: Produced underwater in social contexts; may convey submissive or distress-like signals, particularly in subordinate males or females in close-range social situations.
acoustic_description: A prolonged descending tonal call with a slow gradual frequency decline; longer and smoother than the whistle-descending type; moaning quality with relatively low frequency content.

semantic_description: Produced in close social contact contexts, particularly by females near pups or in affiliative adult interactions; analogous to soft affiliative calls documented in other phocids.
acoustic_description: A short soft low-to-mid frequency tonal call with a rounded cooing quality; relatively pure tone with limited harmonic structure; quiet compared to display calls.

semantic_description: Male Weddell seals produce individually stereotyped multi-element call sequences (songs) used for underwater territorial advertisement and courtship during breeding season; seven distinct male song types have been described at some sites.
acoustic_description: A structured sequence of multiple heterogeneous call elements (trills, whistles, chirps, grunts) combined in a stereotyped order; can last many seconds to minutes; individual males produce recognizable stereotyped multi-element sequences described as "songs".

semantic_description: A named call type in the descriptive catalog of Weddell seal vocalizations used in underwater territorial display sequences.
acoustic_description: A two-part compound call consisting of a high-frequency ascending "what" element followed immediately by a low-frequency abrupt "chunk" element; the acoustic contrast between the two components is striking.

semantic_description: Main adult male breeding-season signal used to attract females and broadcast occupancy to nearby males in choruses.
acoustic_description: A loud low-pitched multi-note bellow or rumbling drone, often rendered as jug-o-rum, built from several quasi-harmonic croak notes in sequence.

semantic_description: Used by resident males to signal that a site is occupied and to challenge intruding bullfrogs before or during territorial escalation.
acoustic_description: A shorter low-pitched challenge call distinct from the long advertisement bellow and lacking the full multi-croak jug-o-rum sequence.

semantic_description: Used in male-male conflict and territorial escalation when a rival approaches or social tension rises in the chorus.
acoustic_description: A shorter, more abrupt, spit-like call than the advertisement bellow, lacking the prolonged multi-croak structure.

semantic_description: Given during close approach and assessment between rival males, typically early in an agonistic interaction.
acoustic_description: A brief call type associated with close social encounters, simpler and shorter than the advertisement call and often given in rapid interaction sequences.

semantic_description: Produced when an individual is clasped and needs to terminate unwanted amplexus or forceful grasping.
acoustic_description: Short repeated protest-like calls with simple abrupt structure rather than a long resonant bellow.

semantic_description: Heard when a startled individual, especially a juvenile at the water edge, flees or dives suddenly after disturbance.
acoustic_description: A sudden high sharp squeak, much shorter and higher-pitched than breeding calls.

semantic_description: Produced mainly by males in courtship and sexual display.
acoustic_description: A learned, phrase-structured song made of repeated syllable sequences with rich variation.

semantic_description: Used in pair or flock contact, especially when individuals are separated.
acoustic_description: A brief but salient tonal contact call with clear harmonic structure.

semantic_description: Used in routine close-range social interaction.
acoustic_description: A local conversational sequence of short notes with less formal structure than full song.

semantic_description: Produced by juveniles to solicit food and care.
acoustic_description: A repeated high-pitched solicitation call typical of dependent young.

semantic_description: Used in acute disturbance or handling-like contexts and distinguished from routine contact calls in Bengalese-finch call studies.
acoustic_description: A short sharp vocalization, harsher and more urgent than the ordinary distance call.

semantic_description: Used in close-range pair or flock coordination under low arousal.
acoustic_description: A brief simple social call shorter and less carrying than the main distance call.

semantic_description: Used in routine close social interactions among pair-bonded or flocked birds.
acoustic_description: A compact short call type distinct from the distance call in contour and local social deployment.

semantic_description: Produced in response to aerial predators or sudden disturbance near the nest; louder and sharper than routine contact or distress vocalizations, triggering flock vigilance or flight.
acoustic_description: A sharp, loud, brief call produced at high intensity; acoustically distinct from the softer contact calls and more urgent than routine distance calls.

semantic_description: Used in long-range social contact and coordination among family members and allies.
acoustic_description: A low-frequency, often infrasonic call with sustained harmonic structure and prolonged duration.

semantic_description: Produced in excitement, alarm, aggression, or distress.
acoustic_description: A loud resonant arousal call with strong upper harmonics and conspicuous onset.

semantic_description: Associated with aggressive display and intense disturbance.
acoustic_description: A harsh broadband call with more noisy energy than a rumble.

semantic_description: Used in immediate vigilance and short-range alerting.
acoustic_description: A short expulsive sound with broad spectral energy and abrupt onset.

semantic_description: Used especially in close-range interactions involving calves or tightly associated individuals.
acoustic_description: A short higher-pitched call contrasting with the lower-frequency rumble and more forceful trumpet.

semantic_description: Used in reunions and close affiliative greeting contexts to maintain social bonds.
acoustic_description: A low rumble with smooth contour and lower amplitude than a trumpet, often rich in harmonic energy.

semantic_description: Included because African elephant ethograms explicitly list bark-like calls among the common higher-frequency vocal categories used in disturbance and forceful social contexts.
acoustic_description: A short explosive harsh call with a sharper onset than a roar and much less sustained tonal structure than a rumble or trumpet.

semantic_description: Included as a broad distress-oriented class because African elephant vocal summaries often distinguish cries from barks, roars, snorts, and trumpets.
acoustic_description: A plaintive, high-arousal call with a strained noisy quality and longer duration than a bark.

semantic_description: Produced in calm social contexts and during low-intensity interactions; listed in systematic repertoire surveys as a distinct call type separate from rumble, roar, and bark.
acoustic_description: A brief low-frequency call with noisy spectral energy, shorter and softer than a roar and less harmonic than a rumble; often occurs singly or in short bouts.

semantic_description: Constantly produced by males in musth; thought to acoustically advertise hormonal and reproductive state to other elephants, including sexually receptive females and rival males.
acoustic_description: A stereotyped low-frequency, highly harmonic rumble produced continuously or at short intervals; has a distinctive low fundamental frequency and strong tonal quality that differentiates it from general contact rumbles.

semantic_description: Used in rallying and coordinating pack members before movement or hunts and in maintaining contact when animals are separated.
acoustic_description: A low resonant call with relatively smooth tonal quality, often repeated in bouts and carrying farther than the higher social calls.

semantic_description: Used in close-range social interactions and pack-level social excitement.
acoustic_description: A light high-pitched social call composed of repeated brief notes.

semantic_description: Used especially by pups or subordinates soliciting food or social attention from pack members.
acoustic_description: A louder more insistent high-pitched repeated call series than ordinary twitters, with stronger arousal and persistence.

semantic_description: Produced in conflict, handling, injury, or acute distress situations.
acoustic_description: A sharp high-intensity call with strong distress or protest quality.

semantic_description: Used in close-range social interaction, including food-begging and socially directed solicitation.
acoustic_description: A low rough call with deeper, more sustained structure than a squeal or twitter.

semantic_description: Used in close-range warning and competitive interactions.
acoustic_description: A rough low call with threat-like quality and variable duration.

semantic_description: Used in alarm, disturbance, and high-arousal rally contexts.
acoustic_description: A short harsh abrupt call with broad spectral energy, structurally simpler than the long hoo call.

semantic_description: Used in close-range social contact, appeasement, and some food-soliciting or dependent interactions.
acoustic_description: A thin high-pitched tonal call that is less explosive than a squeal and usually less insistent than a begging cry.

semantic_description: Reported in some social and food-transfer contexts, but it appears relatively uncommon compared with hoo calls, twitters, or begging cries.
acoustic_description: A low soft sustained call with smoother contour and less harshness than a growl or rumble.

semantic_description: Used during pack rallies as part of collective decision-making before departures or hunts.
acoustic_description: A very short explosive nasal sound that can occur in repeated bursts during pre-departure rallies.

semantic_description: Used in low-arousal social contact, vocal exchanges, and friendly coordination between separated partners.
acoustic_description: A smooth tonal call with harmonic structure and a relatively long, often gently modulated contour.

semantic_description: Used in routine social communication, especially during approaches and uncertainty-reducing interactions.
acoustic_description: A short lower-pitched call simpler and more abrupt than the coo.

semantic_description: Common in affiliative female interactions and infant-related contexts, especially where tension reduction or friendly intent matters.
acoustic_description: A soft high-pitched call, usually brief and often given in repeated affiliative series.

semantic_description: Most typical of infants and juveniles in distress, protest, or solicitation contexts that recruit maternal or nearby social attention.
acoustic_description: A harsh high-pitched distress call, often given in rapidly repeated bursts and acoustically rougher than girneys.

semantic_description: Common in severe conflict and victim responses.
acoustic_description: A loud high-arousal distress vocalization with strong noisy energy and variable contour.

semantic_description: Used in aggressive displays and other high-arousal antagonistic interactions.
acoustic_description: A short harsh call with abrupt onset and broader spectral energy than coos, grunts, or girneys.

semantic_description: Given around copulation and other sexual interactions.
acoustic_description: A conspicuous repeated sexual call series distinct from routine social contact calls.

semantic_description: Produced during aggressive threat displays directed at subordinates or rivals; frequently accompanies head-raised ear-forward threat posture signalling increased intention to attack.
acoustic_description: A brief (~300 ms) harsh noisy call, often produced in rapid bursts, with a rough-sounding texture lacking clear tonal structure.

semantic_description: Produced in medium-arousal threat and spacing contexts; also documented during phonatory physiology recordings and spontaneous captive sessions.
acoustic_description: A low-pitched continuous rumbling call with rough noisy quality, longer in duration than pant threats.

semantic_description: Produced upon discovery of preferred or high-quality food items; may recruit group attention to food patches.
acoustic_description: A brief high-pitched harmonically rich call with a rising or arched frequency contour (~500 ms), related to the warble/harmonic-arch family of food-associated calls.

semantic_description: Associated with discovery of rare or high-quality food; functionally overlaps with chirps and harmonic arches; documented in the context of food broadcasting across macaque species.
acoustic_description: A relatively long (~500 ms) harmonically structured call with a frequency contour that rises toward the middle or end; acoustically richer and more sustained than chirps.

semantic_description: Given by estrous females, particularly during mate-solicitation and around consort interactions; Green (1975) identified a distinct coo variant specific to estrous females.
acoustic_description: A distinctive high-pitched tonal call produced by females; acoustically separable from routine social contact calls; may show variation correlated with reproductive state.

semantic_description: Emitted by infants during separation from mother or in distress; mothers respond selectively to their own infant's version; functions to re-establish physical contact.
acoustic_description: A clear high-pitched tonal call produced by young infants, often with a rising contour; individually distinctive enough for mothers to recognise their own infant.

semantic_description: Produced during mid-arousal conflict interactions; associated with submission or protest by lower-ranking individuals receiving aggression.
acoustic_description: A high-pitched sustained tonal call louder than girneys and acoustically intermediate between coos and screams in arousal level; may show graded transition into full screams.

semantic_description: Produced by subordinate individuals during approach by or interaction with dominant animals; typically accompanies the silent bared-teeth (grimace) expression signalling non-aggression.
acoustic_description: A brief quiet call associated with bared-teeth submission facial display; softer and less intense than squeals or screams.

semantic_description: Used in low-arousal social contact, friendly coordination, and some food-associated situations.
acoustic_description: A relatively tonal call with harmonic structure and a smooth, often gently modulated contour.

semantic_description: Used in routine social communication, especially during approaches and friendly interactions.
acoustic_description: A short lower-pitched call simpler than a coo and often given in brief repeated series.

semantic_description: Often linked to female affiliative exchange, interest in infants, and tension reduction.
acoustic_description: A soft high-pitched call often delivered in repeated affiliative sequences.

semantic_description: Typical of infants and juveniles in distress, protest, and solicitation contexts that recruit maternal or nearby social attention.
acoustic_description: A harsh high-pitched distress call, usually produced in repeated bursts and rougher than girneys.

semantic_description: Common in intense conflict, especially from victims and subordinates during attacks, chases, and aid-recruitment episodes.
acoustic_description: A high-arousal scream with broad noisy energy, irregular contour, and less tonal structure than arched scream variants.

semantic_description: Produced in agonistic episodes and separation-rejection contexts, especially where conflict severity or rank-related distress is high.
acoustic_description: A loud partially tonal scream with a pronounced rise-then-fall or arching frequency contour, often more structured than noisy screams.

semantic_description: Used in aggressive displays and other antagonistic high-arousal interactions.
acoustic_description: A short harsh call with abrupt onset and broader spectral energy than coos, grunts, or girneys.

semantic_description: Typical alarm or sudden-threat vocalization, often given in threatening situations rather than routine social aggression.
acoustic_description: A single loud, high-pitched bark that is sharper and more piercing than the broader harsh aggressive bark.

semantic_description: Given during or around copulation and other sexual interactions.
acoustic_description: A conspicuous sexual call series, usually louder and more aroused than affiliative contact calls.

semantic_description: Associated especially with high-quality or rare food discoveries and may attract nearby group members.
acoustic_description: A harmonic contoured call, often with a rising and falling melodic shape and longer duration than grunts.

semantic_description: Produced to especially preferred foods and treated by playback work as part of the rhesus food-call system.
acoustic_description: A harmonic call with an arched contour that rises toward the middle or end before falling again.

semantic_description: Given particularly to high-quality foods and likely contributes to recruitment or socially informative food signalling.
acoustic_description: A relatively short high-pitched harmonic food call with a compact modulated contour.

semantic_description: Reported as part of the species-typical contact/play movement repertoire, especially in contrast to the more tonal coo.
acoustic_description: A rougher, harsher short call than a coo, with reduced tonality and a more guttural sound quality.

semantic_description: Used in agitated aggressive encounters, surprise, and some juvenile high-arousal interactions, with boundaries that likely grade into screams and geckers.
acoustic_description: A brief sharp high-pitched call, often harsher and shorter than coos or girneys and less sustained than full screams.

semantic_description: Associated with escalating aggression, close-range threat, and attack-related displays.
acoustic_description: A low rough pulsed call with growly or rattling quality and stronger nonlinear harshness than grunts.

semantic_description: Used in overt threat displays and aggressive face-to-face confrontations, often as part of a multimodal aggressive signal.
acoustic_description: A repeated harsh expiratory series or pulsed threat call, typically shorter-unit and more rhythmically repeated than a growl.

semantic_description: Produced in response to disturbances in the environment, including approach of conspecifics from other groups or predators. Receivers respond with vigilance or flight. Call variation correlates with stimulus type, suggesting graded referential function.
acoustic_description: A loud, sharp, high-pitched call with rapid frequency modulation. Short duration, abrupt onset and offset, often with a downward frequency sweep. Acoustic structure varies with the nature of the eliciting stimulus, distinguishing two subtypes (e.g., intergroup vs. predator contexts).

semantic_description: Produced by infants and juveniles seeking to re-establish contact with a social group or specific individuals, or during mild distress situations such as separation or competition. Recruits attention from group members.
acoustic_description: High-pitched, noisy, broadband vocalisation often produced in rapid bursts or sequences. Irregular frequency contour; substantial energy spread across frequencies indicating noise or aperiodicity. Relatively short individual units repeated in quick succession.

semantic_description: Produced during intense social conflicts, submission, or high-arousal distress. Highly undulated screams are most often given by infants and juveniles and rarely by adults. The graded structure allows encoding of varying urgency and social contexts including submission and active attack.
acoustic_description: Loud, high-frequency call with substantial noise and broadband energy. May be tonal or noisy depending on intensity and context; undulated variants show rapid amplitude or frequency modulation producing a wavering quality. Duration is moderate to long; often produced in sequences. Graded between noisy and tonal extremes.

semantic_description: Produced during relaxed social interactions, proximity between individuals, or low-key contact maintenance within a group. Functions to signal benign social intent and maintain cohesion. Common in affiliative and approach contexts.
acoustic_description: Low-pitched, relatively quiet, short harmonic call. Fundamental frequency typically below 500 Hz with clear harmonics. Duration brief (under 200 ms per unit). Graded in quality toward pant-grunt or girney at extremes.

semantic_description: Produced primarily by adult females during interactions with infants, including infant handling and huddling. Functions in caregiving and affiliation contexts between adult females and infants; may reinforce maternal bond or signal benign intent during alloparental care.
acoustic_description: Nasally-sounding, noisy call with irregular frequency modulation, giving it a rough or buzzy quality. Short duration units; may be repeated. Distinct nasal resonance distinguishes it from clean grunts.

semantic_description: Produced occasionally during group movement or spacing contexts; likely functions in long-distance contact maintenance or coordination within and between group members. Less common than screams or grunts but documented as a distinct call type in the repertoire.
acoustic_description: Tonal, relatively pure-tone call with clear harmonic structure and smooth frequency contour. Duration moderate to long; low-to-medium frequency. Occasionally produced as isolated units; described as "coolike" in accounts of the Barbary macaque repertoire.

semantic_description: Produced during submissive or affiliative approaches toward dominant individuals, or during relaxed close contact. Signals non-threatening intent and social tolerance. Part of the graded continuum between grunt and submissive calls.
acoustic_description: Low-frequency pulsed call produced in rapid rhythmic bursts synchronised with breathing (respiratory panting). Individual pulses are short and quiet; the series can be sustained for multiple seconds. Intermediate between pure grunt and rapid grunt series.

semantic_description: Produced by females during copulation. Function debated: proposed to incite male-male competition for access to the calling female, and to influence the probability of male ejaculation. Call timing and presence versus silence influence mating outcome. Acoustic parameters correlate with estrogen and progesterone levels across the cycle.
acoustic_description: Loud, high-pitched, tonal to semi-tonal calls produced in series or trains during copulation. Units are short to medium in duration with upward or complex frequency sweeps; repeated multiple times per copulation bout. Acoustic structure varies with reproductive state (hormonal correlates documented).

semantic_description: Given to warn group members of potential threats, especially predators. Elicits vigilance, flight, or mobbing responses in receivers. Described specifically in the literature as a loud, high-pitched warning call used to alert the troop to danger.
acoustic_description: Loud, high-pitched call often described as an "ah-ah" sound; produced in rapid sequences. Each unit is short with abrupt onset; sequences can be sustained or repeated at intervals. Overlaps acoustically with shrill bark but may be produced in distinct predator-specific contexts.

semantic_description: Produced as a signal of appeasement and non-aggressive intent during interactions with dominant individuals or during affiliative approaches. Often occurs alongside lip-smacking; communicates social tolerance and submission, reducing aggression.
acoustic_description: Rapid, low-amplitude, pulsed sound produced by the teeth and lips; individual clicks or pulses at high repetition rate. Very short overall duration per bout or sustained in sequences. Low-intensity; often heard only at close range. Accompanied by a distinctive visible facial gesture.

semantic_description: Produced by infants separated from their mother or social group. Mothers and group members respond to the call; mothers can individually recognise their infant's calls. Functions to restore mother-infant proximity and recruit caregiving attention.
acoustic_description: High-pitched, tonal to semi-tonal call of moderate-to-long duration. Smooth or slightly modulated frequency contour; higher fundamental frequency than adult calls. May be produced as single units or brief series. Acoustic structure encodes individual identity allowing recognition by the mother.
